title: Semidefinite relaxations of fractional programs via novel convexification techniques
contribution: Derives the concave envelope of x/y over a rectangle in closed form, and the convex envelope as a disjunctive hull of the faces x = xL and x = xU that can be written as an SDP or a second-order-cone system. Shows that the convex envelope strictly dominates earlier underestimators, and that the Zamora-Grossmann inequality is the envelope when y has no upper bound. Extends the recipe to (ax+by)/(cx+dy), to functions concave in x and convex in y, to f(x)y², f(x)/y and to sums. No computation.
problem_entry: The envelopes of x/y over an arbitrary rectangle were still open. Global methods linearized zy = x, and the Grossmann group's nonlinear inequalities showed room for improvement (p. 2).
key_idea: Locate the generating set: the corners for the concave envelope, the faces x = xL and x = xU for the convex one. Take the tightest extension over it and convexify by disjunctive programming, using the perspective substitution and an auxiliary variable. Then rewrite the result by Schur complements as an SDP or a second-order-cone system (pp. 4-7, 13-14).
assumptions: A rectangle in the positive orthant (§§3.1-3.3); 0 ∉ [yL, yU] suffices (§3.4, pp. 11-13). For §4, f is l.s.c., concave in x, convex in y and bounded (pp. 15-16). For §3.6, nonnegative coefficients and ad > bc (p. 14).
proof_devices: generating-set theorems of S028, used without re-proof (Theorems 2.2-2.4, p. 3)
convex disjunctive hull of two faces, with the perspective substitution yp = ya(1 − λ) and an auxiliary zp that removes the singularity on the faces (pp. 6-7, 16)
KKT analysis of the one-dimensional problem (C) in yp, giving the closed forms (13)-(14), the infeasibility of (11) and Theorem 3.4 (pp. 9-10)
Schur complements and the rotated-cone identity (25) (pp. 13-14)
Rikun's theorem for separable sums (Theorem 4.1, pp. 19-20)
experiments: none; worked numerical examples only (Examples 3.1-3.3 and 3.5, pp. 7-8, 11)
positioning: Written against the Grossmann group's relaxations of x/y. The Quesada-Grossmann inequalities leave room for improvement, and the Zamora-Grossmann concave envelope is re-proved by a different route. Their underestimator turns out to be one piece of the new envelope, and the envelope over [xL, xU] × (0, ∞) (pp. 2, 10).
writing: Strict dominance is argued with example points; coincidences are flagged first and explained later (pp. 7-8, 10). Two claims go further than the paper shows: a systematic means for general factorable programs (p. 14), and the dismissal of the vector-x case without proof (p. 16).
limits_future: No algorithm, implementation or computation. The algorithm is not detailed (p. 2), and SDPs inside branch and bound are left as ongoing research (p. 20). Future directions: SDP instead of LP relaxations for factorable programs, and approximation algorithms for fractional programs (p. 20).

method_links.note: Dated (2001). Proposes solving SDPs instead of the traditional LP relaxations, on the grounds of strength and polynomial solvability, with no evidence on time, failures or the search tree. The 2005 paper reversed this on speed and robustness. In the same period S053 (listed here as a 1999 manuscript) chose an LP relaxation by gap and CPU time. Updates the a2-02 abstract-level reading (variant).
Theory with no code. A global algorithm could be built along the lines of [30, 35] ([30] is the authors' own MINLP study) but is not. Nothing in the text shows that the relaxation entered BARON.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one framework re-derives the zoo, then extends it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The Zamora-Grossmann underestimator is recovered as one piece of the envelope, and as the whole envelope when y has no upper bound (Theorem 3.4). Their concave envelope is re-proved, and each earlier inequality is shown to be strictly weaker at some point. The recipe then covers four more function classes.

Characterize the generating set and view the envelope as the tightest extension over it. Convexify the finite union of convex pieces by disjunctive programming, then rewrite the result in a tractable cone. The paper states this as its basic technique on p. 3. The theory is in S028, and S053 uses the vertex case.

transferable: Take a function over a box that is linear or concave in x and convex in the other variables. Write its convex envelope as the disjunctive hull of the faces x = xL and x = xU, using the perspective substitution yp = ya(1 − λ) (pp. 5-7, 15-16).

If a perspective form divides by zero on a face, add an auxiliary variable so the system stays valid there. Then write each zy ≥ x² constraint as a 2×2 LMI or a rotated second-order cone (pp. 7, 13-14).

Get closed-form envelope pieces from a KKT analysis of the one-dimensional disaggregation problem: interior stationary points give one family, the bounds give the rest. Drop the branches that are never feasible (pp. 9-11).

Replace a function by a simpler one that agrees with it on the generating set; both have the same envelope. Examples: the bilinear interpolant of the corner values (p. 5), and the linear interpolant of f for f(x)/y (pp. 18-19).
Prove strict dominance over earlier inequalities with small numerical points at which each lies strictly below the new envelope. Then explain where they coincide (pp. 7-8, 10).

quotes.text: As a result, new algorithms may be developed for factorable nonlinear programming problems incorporating these relaxations and solving semidefinite programs instead of the traditional linear programming relaxations.
A global optimization algorithm using this relaxation scheme may then be easily constructed along the lines of [30, 35] and shall not be detailed in this work.

title: Convex extensions and envelopes of lower semi-continuous functions
contribution: Defines convex extensions of l.s.c. functions and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence. Identifies the tightest extension, and shows that it is the convex envelope iff the generating set lies in the prescribed set. Gives local tests for the generating set and treats the multilinear (vertex) case. Derives the exact maximum gaps of three underestimators of x/y over a rectangle: the convex envelope, the Zamora-Grossmann underestimator and the McCormick-based one.
problem_entry: Tight convex relaxations are central to the efficiency of global optimization (p. 1). The paper generalizes Crama's concave extensions of 0-1 functions to l.s.c. functions that a convex function must match on an arbitrary subset (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: A convex extension exists iff, at each point of X, φ is at most every convex combination of its values at points of X that average to that point (Theorem 2). The tightest one is the envelope of φ set to +∞ off X (Theorem 5), and it equals the envelope over C iff the generating set lies in X (Theorem 6). A point can be excluded from the generating set by a local argument (Theorem 7, Corollary 5). For multilinear functions the generating set is the vertex set, so vertex data extend through the multilinear interpolant (Theorems 8 and 10, Corollary 6) (pp. 3-11).
assumptions: φ lower semi-continuous (p. 2); a compact convex C for the generating-set results (pp. 7-8); no infinite two-sided directional derivative in Theorem 4 (p. 5); twice differentiability and existing multipliers for the second-order argument (pp. 5-6); x/y on a rectangle in the positive orthant (p. 11).
proof_devices: Rockafellar's face theorem (Theorem 18.3) and representation theorem for closed convex sets (pp. 2, 7)
dimension counting by contradiction for faces of epigraphs (Proposition 1, pp. 2-3)
supporting-hyperplane test for where the envelope touches the function, with a second-order corollary (Theorem 4, Remark 1, pp. 5-6)
smallest counterexample separating the envelope from the tightest extension: x² on [0, 1] restricted to {0, 1} (p. 5)
reduction of a multilinear form to a bilinear form with a matrix that is not positive semidefinite (Theorem 9, p. 10)
explicit multilinear interpolant built from product weights (Theorem 10, p. 11)
closed-form maximum gaps, by monotonicity in one variable (Theorems 11, 13, pp. 13-15) and by convexity of the gap on two quadrilaterals (Theorem 12, p. 14)
max-gap models with the inner envelope evaluation replaced by its KKT conditions, solved to global optimality (models OC, OG, CG, pp. 15-16)
experiments: One box, [0.1, 4] × [0.1, 0.5]. Maximum gaps: 3.38 for the envelope, 7.09 for Zamora-Grossmann, 14.13 for the McCormick-based underestimator and 5.72 for the maximum of the last two. Gaps with no closed form come from max-gap models solved globally with the group's solver (BARON). Nothing is timed (Table 1, pp. 15-16).
positioning: Generalizes Crama's definition (p. 3) and recasts Rikun's multilinear polyhedrality result in terms of generating sets (p. 9). Measures itself against the McCormick/Al-Khayyal-Falk outer-linearization and against Zamora-Grossmann (pp. 2, 12).
writing: Theorem-proof, with one worked application and no conclusion section (p. 16). The words 'much tighter' and 'significantly tighter' rest on that one box (pp. 1, 2, 16). Table 1's gap column matches the closed forms, but two of its x*/y* entries do not match their points: 10.2077 at (2.05, 0.1) and 22.6014 at (4, 0.17968) (p. 16; my arithmetic).
limits_future: Theory only. The generating-set condition is not easy to verify in general, hence the local tests (p. 8). Applications are left to the companion papers on hyperbolic programs, pooling and envelopes (p. 2). No algorithmic claim.

method_links.note: Relaxations are ranked by maximum gap only, in closed form and on one box. Tightness is called central to efficiency, with no time or failure criterion. The winner is nonlinear and the baseline is the LP outer-linearization. Unlike S032, the paper does not propose replacing LP relaxations.

Weak. In this theory paper the group's production solver is the measuring instrument: the max-gap models, one with an embedded KKT system, were solved to global optimality with it (refs. [15] and [4], where [4] is BARON).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one framework re-derives the zoo, then extends it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Crama's extensions become a special case, and Rikun's multilinear polyhedrality becomes a statement about generating sets. The McCormick-based and Zamora-Grossmann underestimators are convex extensions over different sets of faces, and the envelope is the tightest over all proper faces.

The theory behind the recipe: the tightest extension and the envelope coincide iff the generating set lies in the prescribed set, and local tests locate the generating set. It is applied to x/y as a disjunctive hull of two faces.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: add, don't replace (intersect a new relaxation with the incumbent one when neither dominates)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Partial fit. Two older underestimators of x/y, neither dominating the other, are combined as max{zf, zu}, an extension over the union of the faces on which they are exact. This cuts the maximum gap to 5.72, from 14.13 and 7.09. The new envelope (3.38) still beats the combination.

transferable: Before computing an envelope, find where it can touch the function. A point is outside the generating set if it lies in the relative interior of a segment in the domain along which the function is concave (Corollary 5, p. 8), or if it is an interior point where the Hessian is not positive semidefinite (p. 6).

Explain each underestimator by the faces on which it is exact. The tightest extension over the union of those faces dominates, and the maximum of two extensions is an extension over the union of their face sets (Corollary 7, p. 14).

For a function known only at the vertices of a box (for example a function of 0-1 variables), build its unique multilinear interpolant with product weights. Its polyhedral envelope is the tightest convex extension (Theorem 10, Corollary 6, p. 11).

Compute a relaxation's maximum gap in closed form where monotonicity or piecewise convexity allows (Theorems 11-13, pp. 13-15). Otherwise, pose a max-gap problem with the inner envelope evaluation replaced by its KKT conditions, and solve it globally (pp. 15-16).
Separate two notions with the smallest counterexample: x² on [0, 1] restricted to {0, 1} has the extension x but the envelope x² (p. 5).

quotes.text: Central to the efficiency of global optimization methods for nonconvex mathematical programs is the capability to construct tight convex relaxations.
Models (OC), (OG), and (CG) were solved to global optimality using our nonlinear programming solver [15], [4].

title: Global optimization of 0-1 hyperbolic programs
contribution: Turns sums of ratios of linear functions of binaries into eight exact mixed-integer convex (mostly linear) reformulations, using convex and concave extensions of bilinear terms. Ranks them by a dominance graph and by measured gap and CPU time. Solves the cardinality-constrained case with a BARON-based branch and bound that recomputes the ratio bounds and rebuilds the reformulation at every node (node tightening). It needs fewer nodes than CPLEX 6.0 on the root reformulation on 94 of 104 instances, and solves a 58-binary restaurant-location model globally in 5.5 hours.
problem_entry: Constrained multiple-ratio 0-1 hyperbolic programs had received relatively little attention: Saipe's branch and bound and Li's and Wu's MILP reformulations. A blind-folded branch and bound on such reformulations converges poorly (p. 2).
key_idea: Write each ratio as a bilinear identity in a bounded variable, and replace each product of a binary and a bounded variable by its McCormick envelopes, which are exact at binary points (Theorems 2.4-2.5, pp. 4-7). Combine forms and valid inequalities into (R1)-(R8) (pp. 7-11). Because the gap is extremely sensitive to the ratio bounds, recompute them over each node's subset and rebuild the reformulation (node tightening, pp. 14, 17-18).
assumptions: Positive denominators (p. 1). Valid ratio bounds; the tightest come from single-ratio subproblems, strongly polynomial only for special structures, otherwise from the Charnes-Cooper LP (pp. 14-17). Binary extreme points for strictness in Theorem 4.1 (p. 12). Sign conditions for dropping extensions (Remarks 3.1-3.3, pp. 8-9). Implemented and tested only for the cardinality-constrained case (pp. 19-30).
proof_devices: the envelope of φ(x, f) splits into a sum of bilinear envelopes, shown by restricting f to its bounds (Theorem 2.4, p. 4)
the envelope of a bilinear form is exact iff each product has a factor at a bound, proved through a strictly concave direction xi ± yj (Theorem 2.5, pp. 5-6)
dominance graph of the eight relaxations, read off the construction (Figure 1, p. 11)
quasi-convexity of the ratios on faces for strictness (Theorem 4.1, pp. 12-13); the Charnes-Cooper bound embedded by adding inequalities (Proposition 4.2, p. 13)
Megiddo's parametric scheme with median finding: a Θ(n) single-ratio algorithm, equivalent to that of Hansen et al. (Proposition 5.4, pp. 14-16)
experiments: Bounds on random CCH instances (coefficients uniform on [1, 1000], five per size; optima from the R8 MILP solved by OSL): average gaps of about 62-208% for Li's reformulation against 0.3-46% for the new ones; the nonlinear relaxations were slower and failed in MINOS (Tables 3-6, pp. 20-25). Branch and bound, BARON with node tightening against CPLEX 6.0 on the root (R7) MIP: fewer nodes on 94 of 104 instances, ties at one node on 5, CPLEX failures on 5 instances with n = 50. CPLEX was faster in CPU on 47 of the 99 instances it solved, all with m ≤ 10 and n ≤ 20 (Tables 7-10, pp. 23, 26-29; my tally). Edmonton: 100 ratios, 58 binaries, p = 10, solved globally in 5.5 h and 79 nodes (p. 30).
positioning: Li's and Wu's reformulations are special cases of (R1) with zero lower bounds (p. 8). On Li's example, (R5) and (R7) cut his relaxation gap by 76.9% and 62.4% (p. 12). Saipe's bound is dominated, and on his Example 3 the (R7) LP gives the optimum at the root (pp. 19-20).
writing: Claims are stated in nodes: 'In all cases' fewer nodes (p. 23), though five instances tie, and the tables 'clearly demonstrate the importance of node tightening' (p. 24). The CPU losses on small instances are in the tables but not in the text. Table 10 lists only instances 2-5 of size 20-20-8 (p. 29). There is no conclusion section (p. 30).
limits_future: No limits or future work are stated, as there is no conclusion section (p. 30). Visible in the text: the 'off' arm is a different solver (pp. 22-23); the bound comparison excludes the time spent deriving the ratio bounds (p. 20); only the cardinality-constrained case was implemented and tested (§§7-8).

method_links.note: Eight relaxations compared on gap, CPU time and failures. The nonlinear ones were slower and failed numerically in MINOS. The LP relaxation of (R7) was chosen by average gap and solution time, although (R8) had a smaller average gap in all 24 size rows at 2.4-5 times the CPU (my arithmetic). This is the 2005 stance practised before it was stated, in the same period as S032's SDP proposal.

Node tightening is range reduction of the auxiliary ratio variables over each node's subset: an exact optimality-based bound for each, from a cheap single-ratio subproblem, followed by a rebuild of the relaxation (steps 1 and 3). Theorem 5.1 characterizes where the envelope tightens when a bound is tightened. Updates the a2-02 abstract-level reading (variant).
Implemented as a module on BARON's user-supplied upper and lower bounding routines (compare the s01 card of S077, pp. 55-61).

The ablation is not a switch inside one code: the 'off' arm is CPLEX 6.0 on the root reformulation, so the effect of node tightening is mixed with the differences between two solvers. The baseline does get the strongest root formulation, (R7) rather than Li's.

Enters a new class with its own method, not with a benchmark. Random instances with optima certified by an exact MILP solve, two literature examples and one application; no public library. The per-instance tables show CPU losses and CPLEX failures that the text does not discuss.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Linearize through discreteness of the domain
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: McCormick envelopes are exact iff one factor of each product is at a bound, so ratios of binaries become exact polyhedral systems with no new binaries.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reformulate at every node, not only at the root
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The full text gives the mechanism: at each node the ratio bounds are recomputed by exact subproblems over the node's subset, (R7) is rebuilt and its LP solved. This takes fewer nodes than the root-only MIP on every instance that needed more than one node, and less CPU time on the larger ones. It is close to Method 1 step 3 and to the S116 candidate, so it is likely to be absorbed into Method 1.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one framework re-derives the zoo, then extends it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Li's and Wu's reformulations, the Charnes-Cooper bound, Saipe's bound and Hansen et al.'s linear-time algorithm all reappear as special cases or dominated bounds of the extension framework.

transferable: For a binary program with ratio terms, introduce one bounded variable per ratio and write each ratio as a bilinear identity. Replace each product of a binary and a bounded variable by its McCormick envelopes, which are exact at binary points: the result is an exact MILP with no new binaries (pp. 4-10).

Generate a family of reformulations by combining forms with optional valid inequalities, and draw their dominance graph. Then measure each one's gap and relaxation CPU time on random instances and choose by both, not by dominance alone (Figure 1, p. 11; Tables 3-6, pp. 21-25; p. 22).

Get node-wise bounds on auxiliary terms from exact polynomial-time subproblems, and rebuild the relaxation at every node (pp. 14-18). Here: Megiddo's parametric scheme with median finding (Θ(n) without constraints) and Saipe's O(np) algorithm under a cardinality constraint.

Publish per-instance tables for both codes: total nodes, the node at which the optimum was found, peak nodes in memory and CPU time. Wins (nodes, large instances) and losses (CPU time on small ones) are then both visible (Tables 7-10, pp. 26-29).
Report when an auxiliary component did not matter: the GA heuristic helped early in the tree, but no substantial deterioration was seen without it (p. 22).

quotes.text: Therefore, in the branch and bound algorithm for (H), we propose to reformulate the problem at every node of the branch and bound tree using the best available bounds.
Comparing the average gap and the solution times of the various reformulations for (CCH) in Tables 3 and 4, it appears that for these problems, reformulations (R5) and (R7) are the most effective.
